item.title: Iran’s Strikes on Base in Jordan Caused Limited Damage, U.S. Officials Say
item.description:
Iran’s bombardment overnight Tuesday of a military base in Jordan used by American forces resulted in “minimal” damage to equipment and caused no deaths, two U.S. officials said on Wednesday.

But the officials warned that some service members may come forward in the coming days to report traumatic brain injuries, a common feature of such strikes.

Eighteen American service members have been killed and scores have been injured since the war began more than six months ago. The Pentagon has provided little information about U.S. casualties unless they were serious, citing operational security.

The barrage of strikes on the base were the latest volley in what is becoming a regular series of tit-for-tat strikes between Washington and Tehran, as Iran’s leaders show a willingness to escalate the conflict.

Iran targeted Jordan after the U.S. military said on Tuesday that it had destroyed five Iranian oil tankers in retaliation for attempted strikes on a U.S. Navy warship.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps called the strikes a “punitive operation” and said that they would “continue,” according to Iranian state media.

The Jordanian military said that it had intercepted 18 of the 20 missiles and that two had fallen in unpopulated areas. But the two U.S. officials acknowledged that the base in Azraq, Jordan, was hit.

The attacks occurred three days after Iran made its first known attempt at striking an American military vessel.

The Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps claimed responsibility for the attacks on a U.S. aircraft carrier and destroyer, saying it fired ballistic missiles at them for “harassing Iranian ships.”

Both countries appear to be stuck in a cycle that is draining U.S. air defenses and deepening Iran’s economic crisis.

As of last month, the Pentagon had used more than 1,500 Patriot interceptor missiles in the war and had fewer than 1,700 interceptors left, according to two people briefed on the stockpile levels who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive military details. The United States produced about 600 interceptors in all of 2025.

At the same time, President Trump’s naval blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, an economically vital waterway, is making it nearly impossible for Iran to ship oil, its main source of revenue.

Mr. Trump has tried to pivot from a military campaign to one focused on choking its economy, but fighting has flared in recent days as each side jostles for control of the strait.

U.S. military officials have vowed to strike three Iranian ships for every two vessels hit by Tehran. But Iran has continued to fire on ships, throttling the world’s oil supply, to preserve one of its biggest sources of leverage.

The result has been a stalemate.

The U.S. military’s Central Command said the Iranian tankers it targeted on Tuesday were “part of a multibillion-dollar shadow network that funds the I.R.G.C. and its regional proxies,” referring to the Revolutionary Guards. It said the attacks came after Iran fired ballistic missiles at a Navy warship twice in two days.

item.title: Election Officials Grapple With Uncertainty as Supreme Court Considers Mail Ballot Plan
item.description:
Election officials in Madison, Wis., mailed 18,000 ballots on Tuesday, more than a week ahead of the state’s targeted date, just to get them out the door. In Weber County, Utah, officials are considering setting up distribution centers for voters to retrieve their mail ballots and bypass the Postal Service completely.

Across the country, election officials are grappling with the confusing implications of the Trump administration’s proposed mail ballot screening plan, which would allow the Postal Service to determine which ballots can be delivered to voters.

A federal judge has halted implementation of the system, which has been challenged as unconstitutional by two dozen states. The Trump administration has asked the Supreme Court to intervene and allow it to go forward ahead of the midterm elections, which will determine the balance of power in Congress.

While they wait for the court’s order, local election officials are trying to sort out how they would comply with the new rules, which would require states to use federally approved envelopes with bar codes unique to each voter and upload voter data to an online Postal Service portal, which is not yet operational.

“Quite frankly, we don’t even really have a way to prepare because we don’t know when that ruling is going to come down, and then we’re going to get state guidance, and then we are crunching up closer and closer to Election Day,” said Lisa M. Deeley, the Democratic vice chair of the Philadelphia City Commissioners, which runs elections and voter registration for the city. The city is planning to start mailing ballots next week.

“It’s just chaos,” she added.

Some states, including North Carolina, Delaware and Alabama, have already mailed out their ballots, raising serious questions about how they could retroactively comply with the new system if it is put into place.

It is not clear whether or how the Postal Service would verify previously mailed ballots if the new rule goes into effect.

“We have not been provided any further information regarding their process for verifying the ballots,” said Kristin Mavromatis, the spokeswoman for the board of elections in Mecklenburg County, N.C.

On Wednesday, the chief election officials in seven G.O.P.-controlled states filed a brief to the Supreme Court, arguing that it was too close to the midterms to make any major changes to how elections are conducted.

The brief, which was signed by the Republican secretaries of state in Kentucky, North Dakota, South Dakota, Georgia, New Hampshire and Kansas, as well as the lieutenant governor of Utah, broke with the Trump administration’s effort to significantly restrict mail voting ahead of the 2026 elections. They were joined by 26 current county and local election officials and five former election officials.

In signing the brief, the secretaries of state in Kansas and South Dakota found themselves on opposite sides from those states’ attorneys general, who were part of a Republican-led state coalition arguing in support of the administration’s mail voting plans. The Missouri Association of County Clerks and Election Authorities also broke with their attorney general in signing the brief.

Their disagreement was not necessarily on the policy; rather, it was on the timing.

“Attempting to implement the rule now will almost certainly lead to mistakes, delays and confusion for both voters and election officials,” the brief states.

Many election experts say the plan could make it nearly impossible for some Americans to vote by mail because it would create impediments to the delivery of their ballots.

“It would be massively disenfranchising, and it would serve no real purpose, because the government didn’t make any showing that this rule is actually going to prevent any fraud, or even that they could put their rule in place,” said Richard L. Hasen, a professor at the University of California, Los Angeles, who specializes in election law.

Mr. Hasen said that the rule would especially hurt rural, disabled and elderly voters who often cannot easily get to polling locations.

Justin Roebuck, the Republican County clerk for Ottawa County, Mich., a conservative district with one-quarter of its voters casting mail ballots, said the rule appeared to do little to accomplish what the Trump administration has argued is its purpose — to increase voting security.

“So we are actually not accomplishing what the end goal was, but we are going to inconvenience millions of voters across the country — certainly, thousands in my community,” he said.

Under the Constitution, states are responsible for carrying out elections. The states that are challenging the Trump administration’s new plan say that it creates a federal role in elections because the Postal Service would reject ballot envelopes that do not comply with the new standards and send them back to local and state officials to fix.

“That comes dangerously close to playing a role in the administration of elections, which the Postal Service has always, always eschewed,” William Hensley, a former Postal Service official who worked with local election officials on best practices for ballot delivery, said.

The Postal Service has denied taking on a new election administration role, saying that states have complete control over voter registration data.

The agency did not respond to requests for comment this week. In a statement on Friday, the postmaster general, David Steiner, said, “Regardless of political party or perspective, we share a common goal: ensuring that Americans can have confidence that their election mail will be handled securely and delivered reliably should their election officials choose to use the mail for ballot delivery.”

Some of the requirements in the rule — such as those that would standardize federal ballot envelopes and create unique bar codes for voters that the Postal Service can easily read automatically — could improve the process, some elections officials and lawyers said. But, they added, it is impossible to accomplish those changes in time for the Nov. 3 elections.

“These are all good things,” said Eric Fey, the Democratic elections director in St. Louis County, Mo. “But if people haven’t been doing it, it can’t be implemented overnight.”

Missouri is one of 12 states that joined the Postal Service in defending the rule in federal court. The state has said it would be able to comply if the Supreme Court gives the Trump administration the green light, although Mr. Fey said he told the state’s top election official that some counties could not comply because they do not have federally approved envelopes or Postal Service bar codes.

In Utah, a deeply red state that votes almost exclusively by mail, some local officials are discussing abandoning mail voting entirely if the Supreme Court allows the Postal Service to restrict the practice.

With envelopes already printed and ballots coming soon, Ricky Hatch, the Republican clerk in Weber County, Utah, said that it is too late for his county to comply with the proposed federal requirements. Officials are considering setting up backup ballot distribution centers.

“We’re going to have to figure out how are we going to get these ballots into the hands of the voters,” Mr. Hatch said, adding: “It will be expensive and challenging and some voters will be disenfranchised, and it will be confusing.”

In their brief to the Supreme Court, the G.O.P. election officials noted that many of the states had already designed and printed their mail ballot envelopes.

Getting new envelopes would normally take four to eight weeks from vendors. A crush of thousands of municipalities needing new materials could stretch that timeline to 12 to 16 weeks, well beyond Election Day in November, the officials noted.

Some election officials have also expressed alarm about the Trump administration’s requirement that states upload their voter data to a Postal Service portal. The Postal Service would then only deliver ballots to those on the lists.

Elections are usually administered by individual counties, and standardizing voter registrations even within a single state is a challenge, local officials noted.

Some Texas counties have struggled with the state’s election management system that was launched last summer, said Dyana Limon-Mercado, the Democratic clerk in Travis County, one of the largest in the state.

Ms. Limon-Mercado said that certain voter registrations have been disappearing from the state system. At one point, the state system did not accept hyphenated names, she said. “I have no confidence that this state system that is also unstable and still buggy is going to connect to some federal system that we haven’t seen yet or tested yet,” she said.

Zach Montague and Nick Corasaniti contributed reporting.

]]>

item.title: Fetterman Has a Surprise Cameo at Trump’s Convention
item.description:
Senator John Fetterman of Pennsylvania, the self-proclaimed champion of working-class voters who has become alienated from his own party and fed up with his job, on Wednesday appeared in a short video on the opening night of President Trump’s midterm convention in Dallas.

“Yes, I’m a Democrat. Why am I here talking to you today?” Mr. Fetterman said in a video filmed in front of a steel mill in Pennsylvania. He introduced himself as a “common-sense Democrat” who said he is “always going to reject the extremes in socialism.”

Mr. Fetterman introduced Senator David McCormick, Republican of Pennsylvania, and said that they would work together “and work with President Trump and defend the steel way of life.”

The appearance of a Democrat at a convention boosting the G.O.P., at a time when his party is claiming that they have made life harder and more expensive for Americans, was a boon for Republicans just weeks before crucial midterm elections in which they are battling to defend their slim congressional majorities.

And it undercut Democrats’ message as they work to focus the final crucial weeks of the midterm campaign on the president, whose approval ratings are sagging, and his unpopular policies. Instead, Mr. Fetterman’s brief comments underscored Republicans’ main argument in the campaign — that Democrats are extremists and socialists who cannot be trusted to govern.

It came amid recent speculation that Mr. Fetterman could switch parties, a move he has said he would “never” make but has appeared more likely as his breaks with his own party have become more frequent and bitter.

His decision to take part in Mr. Trump’s convention appeared designed for maximum shock value and served as a boost for Republicans’ otherwise lackluster gathering, which many of their most vulnerable incumbents and candidates have opted to skip as they work to gain some distance from an unpopular president.

At the height of Mr. Fetterman’s popularity with Democrats, he briefly harbored aspirations to run for president in 2028, according to former aides. Instead, frustrated with his own party and his standing within it, and aware of the attention he garners for criticizing it, he has sought allies on the other side of the political aisle.

In recent months, Mr. Fetterman has amped up his flirtations with Republicans, while still vowing that he would never actually switch parties. In July, he set up an unusual joint fund-raising committee with Mr. McCormick, with whom he has established a close, personal bond. And he has said that if his party officially turned against Israel, as some of its most progressive voices are urging, it would be the “red line” that would force him to leave.

But he has also been adamant that despite his disagreements with Democrats and his antipathy to party gatherings and caucus meetings, he had less in common with Republicans. In an interview in July, he told The New York Times he would “never” leave the party.

About 69 percent of likely Democratic voters in Pennsylvania view Mr. Fetterman negatively, according to a poll conducted last month by The New York Times, The Philadelphia Inquirer and Siena University. Most Republicans in his state, however, now hold a positive view of Mr. Fetterman, who has become a fixture on conservative news outlets bashing the policies of his own party.

The progressive Working Families Party announced last year it would recruit and support a primary opponent to challenge him in 2028.

As Mr. Fetterman has evolved into a lawmaker who barely resembles the man he presented to voters on the campaign trail in 2022 — a champion of the underdog who highlighted his ties to Senator Bernie Sanders, the democratic socialist from Vermont — several former staff members have grown incensed and vocal in saying he is abdicating his responsibilities.

A group of his disillusioned former staff members last week threatened to begin revealing private communications from Mr. Fetterman in which he expressed disdain for the day-to-day duties of being a senator. The former staff members, who made their announcement with an anonymous account on X, said they would begin releasing the material on Monday, when the Senate returned from a weekslong break.

Mr. Fetterman was elected in 2022, after he had a life-threatening stroke in the middle of the most competitive Senate race in the country.

Shortly after being sworn in, he checked himself in to Walter Reed National Military Medical Center to be treated for depression for six weeks, and appeared to make a remarkable recovery as he began speaking out about the importance of getting help when needed. But then in 2024, he began retreating from the job, rarely attending committee meetings, casting votes or holding town halls.

He has since expressed remorse for speaking openly about his mental health and claimed that the criticism he gets for missing votes and committee hearings is because of it.

“My doctor warned years ago: After it’s public that you are getting help for depression, people will weaponize that,” Mr. Fetterman told The New York Times in an interview last year. “Simple things are turned. That’s exactly what happened.”

item.title: Ocasio-Cortez Is Selective About Her Midterm Picks. She Went Far for This One.
item.description:
Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, who has carefully picked which progressive Democrats to support in this year’s midterm elections, quietly made her way to Central Florida on Wednesday to lend her star power to Angie Nixon’s underdog Senate candidacy.

Ms. Ocasio-Cortez encouraged more than 50 campaign volunteers and organizers gathered at a park in Kissimmee, south of Orlando, to devote their time and energy to spreading the word about Ms. Nixon’s campaign — weeks before a single ballot is mailed out.

“They don’t see us coming,” she told them. “My favorite way to move is, we don’t go to the flashy places. This isn’t about fighting for Miami.”

“We run up the numbers here,” she added, “and then we will rack them up everywhere else, too.”

When Florida was still a pre-eminent battleground state not long ago, much of its Democratic energy originated in South Florida. But as that region has grown more Republican, the heart of the state’s progressive movement has moved to Orlando and its fast-growing suburbs.

Ms. Nixon, who is running against Senator Ashley Moody, the Republican incumbent, does not typically hold traditional rallies. Instead, she makes brief appearances intended to sign up volunteers, get them to download a canvassing app and then push them to get right to work calling voters or knocking on doors.

The strategy lifted Ms. Nixon in the Democratic primary last month, when she shocked the party establishment and won by 12 percentage points on a campaign built mainly around field work and social media, despite being vastly out-raised.

That strategy will be harder to pull off in a general election, when candidates have to reach a broader swath of voters, including independents and Republicans, in a big, diverse state that is expensive to campaign in.

Ms. Nixon has challenged Ms. Moody to debate her. On Wednesday, a local Jacksonville television station said Ms. Moody had declined its debate invitation, citing an answer that Ms. Moody gave in a television interview on Tuesday in which she called Ms. Nixon “truly anti-American.” In response, Ms. Nixon called Ms. Moody in a statement “runaway Ashley.”

Ms. Ocasio-Cortez, a potential contender in the next presidential election, endorsed Ms. Nixon last week, but she did not promote her Florida trip. The only news reporter in attendance at the event on Wednesday was a photographer for The New York Times. Ms. Ocasio-Cortez told the volunteers that she had earlier stopped by a local bakery. Kissimmee is heavily Puerto Rican, and Ms. Ocasio-Cortez is of Puerto Rican descent.

“It’s good to be backed by people who are not bought and paid for,” Ms. Nixon said at the event.

Ms. Ocasio-Cortez was introduced by another big supporter of Ms. Nixon’s: Representative Maxwell Alejandro Frost, the first Gen Z member of Congress. Mr. Frost, along with other local officials, has assembled a progressive coalition that campaigns year-round in Central Florida for progressive candidates and issues.

Ms. Ocasio-Cortez promised to defend Ms. Nixon against racist attacks such as the one Laura Loomer, the far-right influencer allied with President Trump, made against her and other Black politicians. (Ms. Loomer described Ms. Nixon and others on social media as “ghetto Black communist,” with a crude epithet tacked on at the end.) That way, Ms. Ocasio-Cortez said, Ms. Nixon — who joined the Democratic Socialists of America in June — might remain focused on campaigning as an unapologetic progressive.

“What we seek to prove,” she said, is that Democrats do not have to run from “some very unimaginative, unambitious place in order to win a statewide election.”

“The way that we do it is by being uncompromising in how visionary and ambitious we want to be for people,” she added. “And to say with our whole chest, ‘We will guarantee health care to every American.’ We can do it without taking big money, we can do without having to compromise our values. We can fight for it all.”

Zack Wittman contributed reporting.

item.title: Democrats Say Fetterman’s G.O.P. Convention Video Had ‘the Persuasiveness of a North Korean Newscast’
item.description:
By now, Pennsylvania Democrats are used to Senator John Fetterman making nice with Republicans. But his 65-second video appearance on Wednesday night at President Trump’s midterm convention ignited a new round of anger and condemnation from Democrats toward a senator they widely view as a political apostate.

Former Representative Conor Lamb, whom Mr. Fetterman beat in the party’s 2022 primary race for Senate, said the video had “all the persuasiveness of a North Korean newscast.”

Mr. Lamb is one of several Pennsylvania Democrats who say they are weighing running for Senate in 2028, when Mr. Fetterman will be up for re-election. Mr. Lamb said party officials in the state had “already assumed Fetterman is a non-factor” in a future race.

Mr. Fetterman has become increasingly estranged from his fellow Democrats since Mr. Trump returned to office last year. While he has remained a reliable vote for Democratic causes in the Senate, Mr. Fetterman has served as a leading cheerleader for Mr. Trump’s war with Iran and for Israel during the conflict in Gaza.

In Washington, Mr. Fetterman long ago stopped participating in routine meetings with Senate Democrats, whom he infuriated by establishing a joint fund-raising committee with Senator David McCormick, the Pennsylvania Republican he introduced in his video on Wednesday.

Polling released last month from The New York Times, The Philadelphia Inquirer and Siena University found that Mr. Fetterman’s popularity with the state’s Democrats had cratered and that he was now far more popular with Republicans.

Mr. Fetterman has said he will “never” switch parties. He did not immediately respond to messages on Wednesday.

Representative Chris Deluzio, a Democrat who, like Mr. Fetterman and Mr. Lamb, hails from western Pennsylvania, said the senator was “making it harder” for state Democrats to win races in November by giving the impression that there is bipartisan support for Mr. Trump.

“If the Republicans want him, they can have him,” said Mr. Deluzio, who said he was also considering a Senate run in 2028. “This guy is not going to be a senator after 2028.”

And Lt. Gov. Austin Davis, who said he had been encouraged to think about running for Senate, accused Mr. Fetterman of misunderstanding the political moment.

“There is a time and place for bipartisanship, but this isn’t it,” he said. “If you willingly participate in this, you’re part of the problem.”

item.title: Republican Senate Candidates Avoid Tariffs and Iran War at Trump’s Convention
item.description:
When Republican Senate candidates took the stage at President Trump’s convention on Wednesday, they steered clear of two big subjects: The war with Iran and tariffs.

Those topics, which have been at the center of Mr. Trump’s presidency, have been politically difficult for Republican candidates in battleground races, with polls reflecting voter frustration, particularly with rising prices that have resulted from Mr. Trump’s decisions.

Mr. Trump, for his part, has encouraged voters to think about the election through the lens of his presidency. “Pretend I’m on the ballot,” Mr. Trump said in his address at the convention.

He defended the war as necessary to prevent Iran from having a nuclear weapon, and said tariffs will revitalize American industries that have lost ground to foreign competitors. (In his address Wednesday night, Mr. Trump said “tariff” is one of his favorite words and that “we will win” the war with Iran.)

But the four Senate candidates from battleground states who spoke on the first day of the convention in Dallas, in keeping with other speakers, did not mention those topics. Instead, they cheered his tax and spending law and praised him in other ways, while often portraying their Democratic opponents as extreme. They were selective in mentioning the president by name.

Here’s a look at their speeches:

Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton: A longtime defender of the president who benefited enormously from Mr. Trump’s backing in the contested Republican primary, Mr. Paxton offered some of the strongest praise for Mr. Trump.

Mr. Paxton named the president five times, saying he “delivered more for this country than anyone before,” and “always stood up for Texas.”

“The press, the courts, and the establishment all tried to take President Trump down, but he has won every single time,” said Mr. Paxton.

Mr. Trump singled out Mr. Paxton in his speech and threw in some affectionate ribbing.

“He may not dress right. He may not talk perfectly. He may not be the best-looking guy I’ve ever seen,” Mr. Trump said. “But you know what he is? He’s the greatest attorney general in America and he deserves to be your next senator.”

Mr. Trump’s super PAC is spending $10 million to help Mr. Paxton as he takes on Democratic nominee James Talarico, a state representative. Polls show a close race.

Senator Jon Husted of Ohio: The incumbent Republican, who is in a competitive race against former Senator Sherrod Brown, a Democrat, mentioned Mr. Trump’s name twice in his five-minute speech — the same number of times he named former President Joseph R. Biden Jr., whom he criticized.

Mr. Husted spoke about how his family “pinched every penny” when he was growing up and highlighted Mr. Trump’s sweeping tax package.

“When you work hard and you earn a dollar, you ought to be able to keep as much of that dollar as possible, shouldn’t you?” he said. “Well, that is the principle behind the Working Families Tax Cut law, which I fought for and President Trump signed into law.”

The legislation cut taxes on tips and overtime and extended child care tax credits for working parents. It also created tax-deferred investment accounts for children, while significantly cutting funding for Medicaid and food stamps.

Former Republican National Committee Chairman Michael Whatley: The Republican Senate nominee in North Carolina mentioned Mr. Trump once by name to praise the president’s tax package. He devoted much of his speech to criticizing his Democratic opponent, former Gov. Roy Cooper, who is showing strength in the polls. Democrats are increasingly confident about flipping the open seat in North Carolina.

The tax cut “put thousands of dollars back into the hands of families and seniors,” said Mr. Whatley, a close ally of Mr. Trump’s who chaired the R.N.C. from 2024 to 2025.

Representative Mike Collins of Georgia: The Republican nominee challenging Senator Jon Ossoff, a Democrat, did not mention Mr. Trump by name. But he spoke at length about the first bill Mr. Trump signed after taking office in 2025, the Laken Riley Act, which requires the detention of unauthorized migrants if they are arrested for certain crimes.

Mr. Collins spent much of his speech criticizing Mr. Ossoff. The incumbent has been leading Mr. Collins in the polls.

Former Representative Mike Rogers of Michigan, the Republican Senate nominee in his state, is slated to speak on Thursday. Representative Ashley Hinson of Iowa said in a Fox News interview over the weekend that she would travel to Texas on Wednesday and return to Iowa on Thursday. She was not on the list of convention speakers published last week.

Senator Susan Collins of Maine and Senator Dan Sullivan of Alaska, two other Republicans in close races, are skipping the convention. So is former Senator John E. Sununu, the party’s nominee in New Hampshire.

Democrats argued Mr. Trump’s low approval ratings would drag down his party’s Senate nominees.

“Nothing they say at this convention will shield them from the reckoning voters are eager to deliver when they elect a Democratic majority in November,” Maeve Coyle, a spokeswoman for the Senate Democratic campaign arm, said in a statement.

item.title: Trump Has Repeatedly Promised Payments That Have Yet to Materialize
item.description:
First, at the start of his second term, President Trump promised a DOGE dividend, a pledge to take the money that Elon Musk’s team would cut from the federal budget and send it to the American people.

Then Mr. Trump moved on to a “tariff refund,” a plan to use the money the government was collecting in import taxes to fund payments for the public.

Those ideas never panned out. Nevertheless, Mr. Trump is again talking up the possibility that the federal government will send Americans thousands of dollars in cash. At the Republican midterm convention in Dallas on Wednesday, the president pledged that every American adult would receive $5,000 if Republicans retain control of Congress in November.

Mr. Trump did not offer many details about the proposal, but there’s reason to think that Republicans in Congress, like they did with his two previous promises of quick cash, could shrug off the president’s suggestion.

That’s in no small part because the $5,000-per-American promise would be enormously expensive to fulfill, with a price tag over $1 trillion. Its actual cost, though, would depend on what, if any, eligibility requirements Congress would ultimately impose on the plan. Mr. Trump did not mention a proposal to finance the $5,000 payments, which beyond their fiscal cost could also prove inflationary.

The conceit of Mr. Trump’s other pitches was that the money to pay for them was already available, from Mr. Musk’s so-called Department of Government Efficiency or tariff revenue. On both of those fronts, though, the envisioned funding sources proved illusory: Mr. Musk’s team did not save the government much money, and the Supreme Court struck down many of Mr. Trump’s initial tariffs.

Republicans did succeed in providing Americans with substantial cash payments when they cut taxes last year. Under the design of the tax law, many Americans first experienced the policy change in the spring, when they received larger-than-usual tax refunds. Mr. Trump and Republicans have spent much of the year promoting those refunds, hoping that the larger lump-sum payments would be politically resonant ahead of the midterms.

But even after Mr. Trump delivered those tax refunds, his approval poll ratings are still sagging.

Those tax cuts were also very expensive, though Republicans did cover some of the fiscal cost by reducing federal spending on health care and food assistance for poor Americans.
